name: Differentiated Materials
title: Differentiated Materials
answer: Differentiated materials is the practice of using AI to produce several versions of the same lesson, worksheet, or reading passage at different levels of support, while the teacher makes sure every version still teaches the same core content. It matters because it saves planning time and lets one lesson reach students who need support, students at grade level, and students ready for a challenge. The teacher remains responsible for checking accuracy, revising rubrics, and confirming that materials fit the class.

sections.body: Teachers often need to teach the same lesson at more than one level, which takes time to prepare by hand. AI can quickly draft three versions of a worksheet or reading passage: one for students who need more support, one at grade level, and one for students ready for a challenge. Tools such as MagicSchool and similar products make this kind of drafting easy. The teacher then checks that each version still teaches the same core content, so the differentiation changes the support rather than the learning goal. The idea solves the planning problem of producing multiple levels without losing the shared purpose of the lesson.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a teacher can give AI the text of a lesson and ask for questions, then check each one for accuracy and clarity, with Google Forms used to deliver the questions and show results. Rubrics can be drafted from an assignment description with levels of performance and clear descriptions, and the teacher revises the rubric to match their expectations and tests it on a few samples of student work. Slide decks can be made by turning a lesson plan into slides with Canva for Education or Google Slides, and video quizzes can be built by embedding a video in Google Forms with questions along the way. AI can also check whether a text's reading level fits a class, though the teacher should confirm by reading it. The text does not give separate grade bands, so these practices apply across the grade levels a teacher works with.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It offers practical guidance rather than research findings, including the observation that a rubric which has never been tested against real work often needs adjustment. It also states that questions drawn from the teacher's own materials are more reliable than questions the tool invents. On that basis, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher stays responsible for the substance of the lesson. Each differentiated version must be checked so that it teaches the same core content, and questions generated from a lesson must be checked for accuracy and clarity. A rubric drafted by AI must be revised to match the teacher's expectations and tested on a few samples of student work, because an untested rubric often needs adjustment. A reading level check by AI should be confirmed by the teacher reading the text. The decisions about what students should learn and what counts as good work remain with the teacher.
